source.title: Feature Hedging: Another way correlated features break SAEs

record.file_problem: The full post text is present. Figures are described but their plotted values are not included in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The post tests overlapping features in narrow toy SAEs and reports a related geometry in LLM SAEs, using SAE reconstruction losses and latent-subspace measurements rather than the original toy-superposition method.
record.gate_note: The post reports toy SAE feature-cosine and loss results, plus measurements of how Gemma-2-2b SAE latents change as width grows. It also reports decoder-bias trends, but describes their interpretation as uncertain. SAE benchmark and Pareto comparisons of loss variants are not recorded as separate rows because the post reports those as performance metrics, not direct measurements of feature overlap or geometry. Results cited from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The post argues and shows that SAE latents need not match true features. Narrow SAEs mix correlated features into latents, and existing Gemma-2-2b SAE latents shift when latents are added. This bears on V5 (SAE features as canonical, stable units). The toy inputs are orthogonal features in R50, so there is no superposition in the data. The study does not test V1, V2 or V4 as stated.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors also claim hedging is caused by MSE loss in any SAE narrower than the true features. They conclude all LLM SAE latents likely contain spurious correlated components, which may explain weak probing and steering performance. They grant that they lack a metric for hedging without growing the SAE.
record.recipe_differences: The post studies narrow sparse autoencoders and reconstruction losses, not the original toy-superposition setup. It uses toy feature distributions, SAE training and measurements of LLM SAE changes as width grows.
record.method_sensitivity: Hedging varies with feature correlation and conditional firing probabilities, L1 penalty, loss choice, whether the parent fires alone, and SAE width. Snap loss fails for stronger correlation and for the parent-with-children-only setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Snap loss (MSE then L2) removes hedging in small toy SAEs but fails at higher correlation, with child-only parents, and shows no clear gain on LLM SAEs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss choice can mitigate SAE feature hedging in low-correlation regimes.

fits_no_version.finding: Decoder bias norm shrinks with SAE width up to about the residual dimension, then grows; in Gemma Scope it correlates with L0. Interpretation uncertain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE decoder-bias norm as an indicator of hedging.

record.peer_reviewed: LessWrong post; the text links a later arXiv preprint, arXiv:2505.11756; peer-review status not stated
record.problems: The exact plotted cosine and loss-curve values are not present in the text. The LLM SAE evidence is indirect: the post says ground truth is unavailable and infers hedging from decoder changes as width grows. Decoder-bias interpretations are explicitly uncertain. Snap-loss results on real SAEs do not show an obvious difference.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. SAE Pareto curves and SAEBench metrics comparing loss variants were left out because the post reports performance comparisons, not direct measurements of the feature overlap or geometry named by the claim.

untested.parts: All of V1. The toy features are orthogonal in R50 with more dimensions than features, so there is no superposition, sparsity transition or geometry.
All of V2. The study concerns SAE latent width, not neuron polysemanticity from model capacity.
All of V4. No measure of feature spreading across neurons or of SAE recovery of the LLM's sparse features.

missing.what: Even with independent features, the decoder bias learns f1 with magnitude 0.2, so hedging appears in the bias.
missing.locator: Case study: single-latent SAEs — Hedging in the decoder bias

missing.what: The portion of change in existing latents drops as the growing SAE gets wider, consistent with hedging decreasing at larger width.
missing.locator: Evidence of feature hedging in LLM SAEs

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked toy SAE rows to V1 and V2. However, the toy data contain no superposition (orthogonal features, 2 to 20 in R50), and the latents are SAE latents, not model neurons. The bearing is on whether SAE dictionary features are faithful and stable units (V5). Snap-loss rows are the study's own method. This LessWrong post precedes arXiv:2505.11756.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test the original toy-model setup, a sparsity-dependent transition, near-orthogonality or regular geometry among superposed directions.
Tests narrow latent capacity and feature sharing, but does not establish a general rule that important features receive dedicated dimensions while less important ones share.
Does not study polysemantic neurons or test causes of polysemanticity other than capacity pressure.
Tests changes in SAE latents on Gemma-2-2b as SAE width increases, but does not test feature spreading across neurons or whether an SAE dictionary recovers all sparse features.
Tests evidence of mixed or changing SAE latents, but does not establish the completeness, stability or canonical status of SAE features generally.
Does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features.

rows.check: Relink to V5. A negative f1 component is merged in, and higher L1 does not remove it.

rows.note: The post also gives an analytical quadratic for this hierarchical case.
rows.check: Analytic loss-landscape result, not a trained SAE. The MSE minimum lies away from the true parent feature.

rows.subject: growing SAE on Gemma-2-2b layer 12 residual stream
rows.size_stated: Gemma-2-2b; SAE starts at 64 latents and grows to 512 latents
rows.operation_detail: Projected changes in existing SAE decoders after adding latents into the subspace spanned by newly added latents; compared with a random 64-latent subspace.

conditions.value: 600M tokens from the Pile dataset at each width

rows.measure: Portion of change in existing latents within the new-latent subspace
rows.baseline: About 2% for a randomly chosen 64-latent subspace
rows.value: About 40–50% of the change in existing latents is in the subspace of newly added latents
rows.locator: Evidence of feature hedging in LLM SAEs
rows.note: The post reports the result across groups of 64 latents; it says the portion of change drops as the SAE gets wider.
rows.check: Remove the V2 and V4 links. The row shows existing latents are not stable as width grows: 40-50% of the change lies in the new-latent subspace vs ~2% for a random subspace. It says nothing about neurons spreading features.

relationships.condition: Narrow standard (MSE/L1) SAEs on correlated, hierarchical or anti-correlated toy features, and a growing L1 SAE on Gemma-2-2b layer 12
relationships.reason: Toy latents merge components of external correlated features (r3, r4, r6, r13, r15, r18), and MSE optima sit off the true feature (r7, r9). Gemma SAE latents change mostly toward new latents as width grows (r20).
relationships.display_finding: Toy SAE latents mixed in components of correlated features they were not meant to track, and the MSE optimum sat away from the true feature direction. In the Gemma-2-2b SAE, latents changed mostly toward new latents as width grew.

relationships.condition: Toy SAEs with independent features, or weak positive correlation with high L1
relationships.reason: Latents recover true features cleanly under independence (r1, r2) or with high L1 and low correlation (r5), so hedging depends on feature correlation structure.
relationships.display_finding: Latents recovered the true features cleanly when features were independent or weakly correlated with high L1, so hedging depended on feature correlation structure.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Toy SAEs with correlated or hierarchical features and a narrow latent bottleneck
reader_labels.reason: The SAE mixes correlated feature components into encoder and decoder latents, and the post reports that greater correlation increases hedging (r3, r4, r15).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Independent features, stronger sparsity for weak positive correlation, and the reported snap-loss toy conditions
reader_labels.reason: Independent features show no interference, sufficiently high L1 can remove low positive-correlation hedging, and snap loss removes hedging in some but not all toy settings (r1, r2, r5, r10-r19).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Toy SAE bottlenecks and the growing Gemma-2-2b SAE
reader_labels.reason: Narrow toy SAEs mix features that are not separately represented, while changes in existing Gemma SAE latents project strongly onto newly added latent directions (r3, r13, r18, r20).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Sparsity and feature-correlation conditions in toy SAEs
reader_labels.reason: Positive hedging can be removed by a high enough L1 penalty when correlation is low, and snap loss helps in some settings but fails under stronger correlation or parent-child dependence (r5, r10-r19).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Growing SAE trained on Gemma-2-2b layer 12 residual-stream activations
reader_labels.reason: The reported decoder changes as width grows are substantially more aligned with the new-latent subspace than with a random subspace (r20).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Toy SAE feature recovery and the growing Gemma-2-2b SAE
reader_labels.reason: Toy SAE latents can contain components of correlated features, and existing Gemma SAE latents change substantially when new latents are added, which argues against treating every SAE latent as a complete, stable canonical unit (r3, r4, r13, r20).
